blocks.text: **The problem.** You're given a grid of `0`s and `1`s with at least one `0`. For every cell, find the distance to the **nearest 0**, counting steps up, down, left or right. Return a grid of those distances.

blocks.alt: Left: the input grid with five zeros and four ones. Right: the answer grid. Each 1 next to a 0 becomes 1. The 1 in the middle of the bottom row has no 0 beside it, so it becomes 2.

blocks.text: The idea: search outwards from the zeros

The question is asked from every **1**: *where is my nearest 0?* Answering it one cell at a time means one search per cell. Turn it around and ask from the **0**s instead: start a BFS from **all of them at once**, exactly like the rotten oranges. Ring 1 of that search is every cell one step from some 0, ring 2 is every cell two steps away, and so on.

BFS reaches cells in order of distance, so the **first** time the search reaches a cell, it has come from that cell's nearest 0. Write the distance down then and never touch the cell again — the distance grid doubles as the visited marker.
1. Brute force: a BFS from every cell
For each 1, run a fresh BFS outwards until it meets a 0. The first 0 it meets is the nearest, because BFS goes ring by ring.

**Time O((m · n)²), space O(m · n).** Each of the m · n cells may run a search that visits most of the grid — a big block of 1s with a single 0 in one corner is the worst case. The searches also repeat each other's work over and over.
Put every 0 in the queue at distance 0 and mark every other cell *not reached yet*. Then run one ordinary BFS: each cell taken from the queue gives its unreached neighbours its own distance plus one.

blocks.caption: One search spreads from every 0 at once; "?" is a cell not reached yet.

blocks.text: **Time O(m · n), space O(m · n).** Every cell enters the queue exactly once and checks 4 neighbours. The queue can hold up to m · n cells — all of them, if the grid is mostly 0s.
3. Two passes: no queue at all

There are no walls, so the distance to a 0 is just *rows apart + columns apart*, and the steps can be taken in any order. That means a cell's answer can be built from its neighbours' answers: it's one more than the smallest of them.

Two sweeps are enough. The first goes top-left to bottom-right and takes the best from the cell **above** and the cell to the **left**, which it has already updated. The second goes bottom-right to top-left and also takes the cell **below** and to the **right**. Every nearest 0 can reach a cell by moving down or right first (carried by sweep 1) and then up or left (carried by sweep 2).

**Time O(m · n), space O(1) extra.** Two sweeps of the grid, and nothing stored besides the answer itself. This trick needs a grid with **no walls** — once some cells are blocked, steps can't be taken in any order and you're back to BFS.

blocks.alt: BFS per cell: O((m·n)²) time, O(m·n) space. Multi-source BFS: O(m·n) time, O(m·n) space. Two passes: O(m·n) time, O(1) extra space.

blocks.text: In an interview, lead with the multi-source BFS: it's the pattern, and it still works when the grid has walls. Mention the two-pass version as the follow-up that saves the queue.

items: **All zeros** — every distance is 0 and the BFS loop does nothing new.
**A single 0 in a corner** — the far corner is the farthest cell, `rows + cols - 2` steps away.
**One row or one column** — the bounds checks must handle a width or height of 1.
**Zeros on opposite sides** — the cells in the middle take the nearer side, which is why all the zeros must start together.
**Map of Highest Peak** — water cells are height 0 and neighbours differ by at most 1: the same search, with water as the sources.
**As Far from Land as Possible** — start from every land cell; the answer is the largest distance any water cell gets.
**Shortest Bridge** — find one island with DFS, then run a multi-source BFS from all of its cells until it touches the other island.
